analytic.title: פרקים במשנתו המשיחית של יהודה הדסי הקראי לקביעת הנוסח של "נפלאות-המשיח" באשכל-הכופר

biblStruct.note: Messianic utterances and slogans are scattered all over the huge encyclopedia of Karaite lore, Eshkol hakkofer, composed by Yehuda Hadassi of Constantinople some time in the middle of the twelfth century. However, the fullest account of the Jewish utopia, as visualized by a Karaite intellectual in the time of the Crusades on the basis of older sources, is given in the last three alphabetical acrostics of that book, from letter waw of Chapter 377 (or, by a different count, 383) till the end of Chapter 379 (= 385). It reflects the extraordinary position which messianism occupied in the outlook of Hadassi and of his contemporaries. The objective of these "Studies" is to compare Hadassi's statement with its counterparts in earlier Karaite literature — in the writings emanating from Babylonia (Qirqisani) or from the Palestinian schools (e.g., al-Qumisi and Yefet ben 'Ali); to weigh it against the messianic teachings prevalent in Rabbinic Jewry; and to view it against the background of Christian-Jewish polemics in Byzantium, notably those of Hadassi's contemporary, the court-theologian Euthymios Zigabenos. Through such analysis, the twelfth-century message of Hadassi's exposition will clearly come to light. Regrettably, a full appreciation of the matter is handicapped by the lack of a critical edition of the Eshkol. The only edition available in print to date — the one published in Czarist Russia [Gozlow] in 1836 — deliberately omitted certain sections dealing with Gentiles (they were edited later, in 1896 and 1941, by Bacher and Scheiber, respectively). However, as already reported by P. F. Frankl some 85 years ago, beside these sections which were marked "Cancelled" in the printed book, several other anti-Christian clauses were tampered with or removed altogether, with no appropriate note indicating the change. Thus, against the original 77 "Wonders of the Messiah", available in all the known manuscripts, the printed book lists only 54. Twenty-three have been tacitly withdrawn and the closing mnemonic formula (simman) camouflaged accordingly. Inevitably, then, the present article is devoted to establishing the full and correct text of Hadassi's "Messianic Wonders", thereby paving the way for the analytical studies to come. The paragraphs missing from the printed copy are published here, for the first time, on the basis of MS Adler No. 1650, at the Jewish Theological Seminary Library of New York, and of MS No. 130 (or No. 53, according to the old catalogue), in the possession of the Nationalbibliothek in Vienna. Also listed are the essential differences between the above manuscripts and those parts of the excursus which were already (uncritically) edited in Gozlow. Now, the Gozlow publication included also an edition of Naḥal ha-eshkol, a Hebrew epitome of Eshkol hakkofer composed in 1497 by Kaleb Afendopolo. This epitome, too, was subjected by the nineteenth-century Russian Karaite editors to self-imposed censorship regarding Christianity. The Appendix to the present article contains, therefore, Afendopolo's synopsis of the 77 "Wonders", as found in the Adler MS No. 14 of his Naḥal eshkol. In the notes a comparison is made between that text and the appropriate section of the still-unpublished seventeenth-century Arabic fihrist of Eshkol hakkofer (MS No. 1750); both manuscripts are in the possession of the Jewish Theological Seminary Library in New York.
